title: The History of Log Flumes — Why America Built 50-Mile Wooden Water Slides
fullText: In 1876, a group of lumbermen in California finished building something that, by all logic, should not have worked. It was a wooden channel, just two planks nailed together in a V-shape, [music] propped up on stilts, and stretched across 54 m of some of the most brutal mountain terrain in North America. The Sierra Nevada canyons hundreds of feet deep. Slopes so steep that mules refused to climb them. And through all of it, this flimsylooking wooden trough carried millions of board feet [music] of lumber using nothing but water and the pull of gravity. It moved faster [music] than any horsedrawn wagon. It cost a fraction of what a railroad would. And it worked so well that it literally built [music] an entire town from scratch at the bottom of the mountain. A town they named MadiRaa, which is the Spanish word for wood. So, how did a couple of planks and [music] a stream of water solve a transportation problem that had stumped an entire [music] industry for decades? The answer starts long before California. It starts with a basic fact about trees that shaped the entire history of American logging. Trees are heavy. A single old growth sugar pine log can weigh several tons. And for the first 200 years of American settlement, there was really only one practical [music] way to move that kind of weight over any real distance. Water. Rivers. You cut the tree down. You rolled it to the nearest creek or river, and you let the current do the work. Loggers would lash logs together into massive rafts and float them downstream to sawmills or shipping ports. The entire early logging industry was built around this one simple idea. stay near the water. And it worked beautifully [music] on the east coast and in the Midwest where rivers were wide, deep, and fairly predictable. Loggers stripped the forests of New England, then moved into the Great Lakes [music] region, floating white pine down rivers that fed into the biggest lumber markets in the country. By the middle of the 1800s, the East Coast timber supply [music] was getting thin. The Midwest was following close behind and lumber demand was only growing because America [music] was building. Railroads, towns, mines, entire cities springing up practically overnight. The country was hungry for wood and the easy wood was running out. That is when the lumber [music] industry turned its eyes west to the Pacific Northwest to the Sierra Nevada mountains of California. And what they found there was both a fortune and a problem. The fortune was obvious. The western mountains [music] held some of the largest, most valuable timber on the planet. Sugar pine, ponderosa pine, douglas [music] fur, and the giant sequoas. Trees so enormous that a single trunk could be wider than a house. The forests seemed endless. They stretched across millions of acres of mountain wilderness, untouched and waiting. The problem was just as obvious. These trees did not grow next to convenient rivers. They grew on the sides of mountains, in deep canyons, on ridgeel lines thousands of feet above the valley floor where the sawmills and railroads sat. And unlike the flat riverfed forests of the east, you could not just roll a log into a stream and let it float to market. Sierra Nevada streams were seasonal. They depended on snow melt, which meant they raged in the spring and dried to a trickle by summer. They were too shallow, too rocky, [music] and too unpredictable to serve as reliable lumber highways. Horse and oxundrawn wagons were technically possible, but the mountain roads were treacherous when they existed at all. Many areas had [music] no roads whatsoever. Building them through canyon country would cost a fortune and take years. Railroads were another option, but a narrow gauge railroad in the 1870s cost around $4,000 per mile to build in mountain terrain. For a 50-mi route, you were looking at [music] $200,000 in $1870. That was enough to bankrupt most lumber operations [music] before they ever shipped a single board. The lumber was there, the demand was there, the money was [music] there, but the space between the trees and the market was a wall of rock and gravity [music] that nobody could seem to crack. Nobody, that is. Until a man named JW Haynes looked at the problem sideways. Haynes had been cutting timber on his land near Kingsbury grade on the eastern slope of the Sierra Nevada since 1866. He understood the mountain. He understood water. And sometime around 1867 or 68, he either invented or perfected a design so simple that it almost seems like a joke. two rough planks, [music] each about 24 in wide and 16 ft long, nailed together at a 90° angle to form a V-shaped trough. You set this trough on wooden supports, angled it slightly downhill, and ran water through it. Then you dropped your lumber in. The water carried it. Gravity did the rest. Now, Haynes was not the first person to use a wooden channel to move things with water. Box flumes, which were basically rectangular wooden troughs, had been around for centuries. The Romans used aqueducts. Miners during the California Gold Rush built box flumes [music] to move water for hydraulic mining. Loggers on the East Coast had experimented with wooden shoots greased with animal fat to slide logs downhill. But the Vflume was different, and the difference matters. The old box flumes had a flat bottom. When a log got stuck, it just sat there. Water backed up behind it. Pressure built and eventually the whole thing either jammed completely or blew out a section of the flume wall. Jams were constant. Maintenance was a nightmare. You needed crews stationed along the entire length just to poke logs free with long poles. The Vshape solved this problem with elegant physics. When a log got stuck in a V flume, the water had nowhere to go but up. As the water level rose behind the obstruction, it lifted the stuck log off the narrow bottom of the V and floated it free. The flume essentially unjammed itself. It was self-correcting. And because the V-shape concentrated the water flow into a narrow channel, you needed less water to keep things moving. You could build a V flume in terrain where a box flume would have been impractical because there simply was not enough water to fill a wider channel. In 1869, Haynes applied for a patent [music] on the design. Whether he truly invented it or simply refined what other lumbermen had been experimenting [music] with is still debated. The Vflume seems to have evolved through trial and error across multiple logging [music] operations in the Sierra Nevada. But Haynes gets the credit because he formalized it, proved it worked at [music] scale, and showed the entire industry what was possible. And what was possible turned out to be absolutely wild. Within a few years of Hannes proving the concept, V flumes started popping up all over the western [music] mountains. And they were not small. These were massive infrastructure projects. Wooden rivers built on stilts that wound through canyons, crossed gorges on trestle bridges 100 ft in the air, and stretched for dozens of miles through some of the most remote wilderness in America. A flume could be built for as little as $300 per mile. Compare that to $4,000 per mile for [music] a narrow gauge railroad. And building was fast. Four men and four [music] oxen could lay a/4 mile of flume in a single day. The economics were irresistible. Suddenly, [music] timber that had been completely inaccessible was within reach, and the [music] lumber companies moved fast. One of the earliest and most important flumes was built in Madera County, California. A man named William Thurman came up with the idea [music] of building a V flume from his mill site near what was then called Fresno Flats all the way down to the railroad head in Madera in the Sanwaqin Valley. Construction started in 1874. 2 years later, the flume was finished. It ran over 50 [music] mi, dropping nearly 4,000 ft in elevation from the Sierra Nevada [music] down to the valley floor. The flume was built in 16 ft sections 5 ft across, consuming every board the Sugar Pine Company could produce during [music] those 2 years of construction. When it opened in 1876, the Madera Flume did not just transport lumber. It created a town. The California Lumber Company [music] laid out lots at the point where the flume met the railroad and they named the settlement Madera. Within months, people were buying property, building homes, and establishing businesses. A newspaper [music] reported that the demand for lots was great. The flume quite literally put Madiraa on the map. Over its lifetime, that single flume carried more than 1 and a half billion board feet of lumber [music] down from the mountains. But the Madera flume was just the beginning. The real monster came about 15 years later. High in the Sierra Nevada, two lumber barons from San Francisco named Hyram Smith and Austin Moore purchased 30,000 acres of timberland in an area known as [music] Milwood. The trees there were extraordinary giant seoas, some of them thousands of years old with trunks so wide you [music] could drive a carriage through them. Smith originally planned to build a railroad to carry the lumber down to the valley. One look at the King's Canyon terrain killed that idea. The canyon walls were too steep, the gorgees too deep, the route too twisted for any railroad ever built. So they decided to build a flume instead. And not just any flume. The longest log flume ever constructed. In 1888, Smith and Moore founded the King's River Lumber [music] Company. Construction began in 1889. By mid1 1890, just 13 months later, the King's River Flume was ready for operation. [music] It ran from the high timber country near Milwood, starting at an elevation of about 4500 ft above [music] sea level and wounded 62 mi down through the rocky canyons of the Sierra Nevada to the lumber yard and railroad depot in Sanger, [music] California. The drop in elevation was over 4,000 ft. The flume was built using the standard V design with planks an inch and a half thick, 24 in wide, 16 ft long, [music] joined at a 90° angle. There were 330 of these sections per [music] mile. Some of the trestle bridges supporting the flume reached heights of over 100 ft. 36 million board feet of lumber were used just to build the flume itself. Think about that. You needed a forest worth of wood just to construct the channel that would carry more wood down the mountain. The operation was staggering in its efficiency. Before entering the flume, the feld sequoas were hauled to a mill near the top, rough cut into planks, allowed to dry, and then clamped together in bundles 12 in square and 18 to 28 ft long. [music] Three to six of these bundles were tied end to end to form what they called [music] a train. and the train was released into the flume. As it wound its way down the mountain, flume herders along the route guided the trains, linking them together into chains as long as 1,000 ft. 15 hours after entering the flume at the top, the lumber arrived at the rail head in Sanger. In its first 4 months, the Kings River Lumber Company shipped nearly 12 million board feet. In 1891, its first full year, [music] the operation shipped almost 20 million board feet. But running a 62-mile wooden channel through the wilderness was not exactly a lowmaintenance operation. The flume herders were the unsung backbone of the whole system. These men lived in small shacks and cabins positioned at intervals along the flume route, often miles from the [music] nearest town or other human being. Their job was to keep the lumber moving and the water flowing. They carried pickaroons, which were metal [music] tipped wooden tools designed for grabbing and maneuvering logs. They watched for jams, cleared debris, patched leaks, and made sure the flow never stopped. On the longer flumes, they communicated using light signals, and eventually telephone lines were strung along the routes so herders could warn each other [music] about incoming trains of lumber or report problems. It was lonely, isolated work, and it was dangerous. The flumes had no guardrails. The catwalks alongside [music] them were narrow planks of wood, sometimes 100 ft above a canyon floor. [music] One slip, one patch of ice, one moment of carelessness, and you were gone. Exact numbers are hard to come by, but early reports describe many falls and many [music] deaths among the men who maintained these structures. And then there was the other thing the flume herders did. The thing that is honestly hard to believe when you first hear about it, they rode the flumes, not occasionally. Regularly, flume herders and other workers would build [music] small wooden boats, basically just planks nailed together into a crude vessel barely wider than the flume channel itself, climb and ride the water [music] down the mountain. Sometimes they did this for legitimate inspection purposes, checking sections of the flume that were hard to reach on foot. Sometimes they did it to get to town faster on their rare nights off. Many of the remote logging camps did not allow drinking, so if you wanted to hit a bar, you had to get down to the valley. Walking could take hours. Riding the flume could get you there in a fraction of the time at terrifying speed through the dark with no breaks. [music] And it was not just the workers. Flume riding became something of a sport in the 1870s and 80s. Wealthy visitors to the Sierra Nevada would pay to ride the flumes for the thrill of it. In the Truckucky area near Lake Tahoe, v Flumes were called Go Devils, and the small boats people rode in them earned the same name. A trendy date in certain mountain communities involved walking along the flume trestles with your companion 100 ft above the ground with no railing to show how bold and courageous you were. If you really wanted to impress, you packed a lunch. Injured or sick workers from remote mountain camps would sometimes be placed in flume boats and sent down to the valley alone [music] for medical treatment. It was the fastest way to get them help. Whether the ride itself did the patient any favors is another question entirely. One newspaper [music] account describes a group of millionaires who decided to ride a flume near Truckucky. Their dugout started down the mountain at high speed. A second boat launched 60 seconds behind them and eventually caught up, slamming into the first boat at the mill pond and sending all four riders flying in different directions. One of the survivors was asked why he did it. His answer was simple. He figured if men worth $25 million a piece could risk their lives, he could too. While flume riding provided some wild stories, the real story of the flumes is one of ambition and consequence. The King's River operation cut down over [music] 8,000 giant sequoas during its 36 years of operation. Some of those trees were over 2,000 [music] years old. And here is the detail that is hard to get past. Of all the trees they felled, only about 23% of the wood ever actually made it to the mill in Sanger. The rest, nearly threearters of everything they cut, was left to rot [music] on the forest floor. The trunks were so massive and so brittle that they often shattered when they hit the ground after being cut. Pieces that were too large or too damaged to process were simply abandoned. It was cheaper to cut a new tree than to salvage a broken one. The environmental destruction was staggering. Entire groves of ancient sequoas, trees that had been alive since before the Roman Empire, were reduced to stumps and debris fields. One tree survived in the midst of all the destruction. The bull tree, still standing today in Converse Basin, surrounded by the stumps and fallen remains of the forest that once stood [music] around it. The irony is that the same operation that devastated these forests, also played a role in creating the national parks that now protect what remains. The public outcry [music] over the destruction of the Sequoia groves contributed to the establishment of King's Canyon National Park and Sequoia National Park. And the water from the King's River Flume did not just carry lumber. It irrigated the fields of the Sanwaqin Valley, helping transform one of the most [music] productive agricultural regions on the planet. The flume built Sanger from nothing. Within a year of the flume reaching town, land values had [music] skyrocketed and a city of 2,000 people had appeared where there was nothing before. The King's River Flume operated from 1890 to 1923. During those decades, [music] it survived floods, fires, bankruptcy, and corporate reshuffleling. The original company went under, and in 1905, [music] the operation was sold to a group of Michigan investors led by Thomas Hume. They renamed [music] it the Hume Bennett Lumber Company, built a new reservoir now known as Hume Lake, constructed a new mill, and extended the flume another 17 mi. In 1917, another bankruptcy hit. A fire destroyed the mill. In 1926, a massive forest fire wiped out [music] 7 mi of Flume. By 1927, it was over. Thomas Hume's son, George, sold [music] the remaining equipment for $20,000. The Madera Flume had a similar arc. After falling into disrepair, it was rebuilt in 1899 by the Madiraa Sugarpine Lumber Company under new ownership. It operated into the early 1930s before the Great Depression [music] finally shut it down. The lumber was scavenged and used to build barns, houses, [music] and fences across the valley. Across the western United States, flume after flume met the same fate. The Shaver Lake flume, 42 mi long, was built in 1893. When a snowstorm crushed parts of it in 1914, it was never repaired. Logging trucks had arrived. They were more flexible, could reach more places, and did not require a constant water supply. Narrow gauge railroads pushed deeper into the mountains. By the time World War II ended, the era of the log flume was over. The wooden channels that had moved billions of board feet of lumber were dismantled piece by piece. Over the decades, scavengers, weather, and forest [music] fires erased what was left. Today, almost nothing remains of these structures. A few preserved sections sit in museums. [music] The Clovis Big Dry Creek Museum has one of the best surviving pieces. The Sanger Depot Museum [music] displays photographs and a half-scale model. Replicas have been built here and there, but the flumes themselves, those miles and miles of elevated [music] wooden rivers that once snake through the Sierra Nevada, are gone. What is not gone is their legacy, and it shows up in a place you would never expect. In 1963, a company called Arrow Development built a ride for Six Flags Over Texas. It was a water channel with small boats shaped like hollowedout logs carrying passengers through a winding course that ended with a big splashy drop. They called it a log flume ride. The original concept had roots in the old chute. The chute's water slides that had existed at places like [music] Coney Island since the turn of the century. But the theming, the winding water channels, the floating boats that came directly from the lumber flumes of the American West, the ride was a massive hit. Within a decade, log flume rides were showing up at amusement parks across the country and around the world. Knottberry Farm built Timber Mountain log ride. [music] Disney created the iconic Splash Mountain. Six Flags Great Adventure added its sawmill log flume in 1974. Today, there is hardly an amusement park on the planet that does not have some version of this ride. Every summer, millions of people climb into fiberglass boats shaped like logs, float through gentle water channels, and plunge down a final drop into a splash pool, screaming and laughing the whole way down. [music] And almost none of them know that they are riding a sanitized, safe, chlorinated [music] echo of something that lumberjacks once did for real at full speed down the side of a mountain in the dark with nothing between them and a canyon floor 100 ft below. The log flumes of the American West were never meant to last. They were built fast, built cheap, and built to solve an immediate problem. Move the wood. get it down the mountain, get it to market. And they did that brilliantly for about 50 years, transforming the western lumber industry, building towns, irrigating farmland, and feeding a nation that could not stop building. They were crude, and they were wasteful, and they destroyed forests that will never grow back. But they were also, in their own rough way, one of the most clever engineering solutions in American history. two planks, some water, and gravity. That was enough to move a forest.
